title: Build Unified Single Paragraphs
outcome: Write one paragraph about one main point, identify what a sentence does and repair or remove irrelevant material. Word guidance is not a quality cutoff.

teaching.lesson1: A paragraph is not simply a block of five sentences. The reader should know what the entire paragraph is trying to explain.
teaching.lesson2: Check each sentence's job against the main point: opening point, reason, example and optional further practical detail. Other coherent orders are possible.

demo.prompt: A neighborhood group is considering a small plant-exchange shelf near the community garden. Explain how it could help neighbors.

steps.label: Notice
steps.text: The paragraph's one job is explaining how the plant exchange could help neighbors.

steps.label: Main point
steps.text: A small plant-exchange shelf could help neighbors share extra seedlings without wasting them.

steps.label: Reason
steps.text: Some households grow more seedlings than they can plant.

steps.label: Concrete detail
steps.text: For instance, a gardener might leave two spare tomato plants for another family.

steps.label: Reject/repair
steps.text: The neighborhood bus fare increased last month does not help explain seedling sharing. Remove it; a shorter, focused paragraph is better.

steps.label: Natural end
steps.text: A simple take-one/leave-one sign could clarify the exchange. A separate summary sentence is optional.

steps.label: Transfer principle
steps.text: Sentence job matters more than length or formulaic Firstly/Finally.

demo.paragraph: A small plant-exchange shelf could help neighbors share extra seedlings without wasting them. Some households grow more seedlings than they can plant, so a shared shelf would give the extras a useful home. For example, one gardener might leave two tomato plants for another family. A simple sign could explain how to take or donate a plant.

teaching.a1: Optional sentence roles: Main point / Why / Example. Use short, understandable sentences.
teaching.b1: Explain when a second detail helps and when it distracts from the central point.

cycleA.prompt: Your school is considering a quiet reading nook near the hallway. Explain why a small space with books and chairs could help students at break time.
cycleA.instruction: For THIS closed task, put the main point first, the reason second, the example before the maintenance detail. Put the off-topic card in Remove. Alternative coherent supporting-detail orders may be explained in your own reflection; this key is not a universal formula.

cards.text: A small reading nook could give students a quiet choice during busy breaks.
cards.rationale: Names the proposal and its central benefit.

cards.text: The hallway can be noisy, so a calmer corner would suit students who want a short reading break.
For example, two chairs and a shelf of short books could fit into an unused corner.
cards.rationale: Makes the proposal imaginable and relevant.

cards.text: A notice asking readers to return books could help keep the nook usable for the next class.
cards.rationale: Offers a possible way to maintain the nook.

cards.text: Our school football team won a match last weekend.
cards.rationale: Does not develop the reading nook's purpose.

cycleA.repairPrompt: Replace X1 with a new sentence that genuinely supports the reading nook. Your wording can differ from the model.
cycleA.reflectionPrompt: What job does S3 perform that S1 does not?
cycleA.orderWhyPrompt: Explain why this order serves a reader. If a different supporting-detail order is still coherent, explain that too.

cycleB.prompt: The school wants to create a student tool-lending corner where classmates may borrow rulers, glue sticks and other safe classroom supplies. Recommend the corner and explain one main benefit, supported with a practical example. Write one coherent paragraph.

strip.topic: School tool-lending corner for safe classroom supplies.
strip.task: Recommend the corner and explain its usefulness.
strip.mustInclude: One main benefit and at least one practical, relevant example.
strip.boundary: School/classmates; safe ordinary supplies; one paragraph.

steps: Write short original planning notes: main point, reason and concrete detail.
Write one original unified paragraph; all sentences should support the same benefit.
Quote one sentence exactly from YOUR paragraph and label its job as point, reason or detail.
Explain why that chosen sentence performs that job. A sentence may do more than one job.
Save your own paragraph version. Suggested length 60–90 words is guidance only.
cycleB.suggestedLength: 60–90 words — guidance only, never a quality cutoff.
cycleB.a1: Optional: I recommend __ because __; For example, __. Do not use as a scored answer.
cycleB.b1: Add a realistic return-supplies limitation while staying on the same paragraph purpose.

transfer.prompt: A local youth center wants one new weekend bicycle-repair pop-up where young people can learn simple, safe maintenance with adult supervision. Write one recommendation paragraph explaining a single benefit, with a concrete example and no unrelated sentences.
transfer.instruction: Write a NEW paragraph and copy one exact supporting-detail sentence from it. The main task is not a word-count test.

supplemental.title: Point versus example
supplemental.prompt: A community pool could offer beginner swimming lessons.
supplemental.question: Which sentence best introduces the overall purpose of a paragraph about this proposal?

options.text: Last Tuesday, a child bought a blue swimsuit.
options.rationale: One incident, not the central proposal.

options.text: Beginner swimming lessons could help new swimmers feel safer and more confident in the pool.
options.rationale: Names the proposal and potential benefit.
Decor does not explain the proposed lesson.

options.text: My cousin prefers cycling to swimming.
options.rationale: Personal aside unrelated to the paragraph.

supplemental.title: Irrelevant support sentence
supplemental.prompt: A neighborhood library wants to lend board games. Paragraph begins: Borrowing board games from the library could help families enjoy activities together without buying every game.
supplemental.question: Which addition is least relevant?

options.text: Families could choose a game for a rainy weekend.
The library could explain how to return missing pieces.
A neighbor bought a red car last year.
options.rationale: Unrelated event, not developing board-game lending.

options.text: Borrowing means families could try different games without owning each one.
options.rationale: On-topic development, though specificity might improve it.

supplemental.title: Concrete rather than empty praise
supplemental.prompt: A school could host a lunchtime music-listening session.
supplemental.question: Which sentence gives strongest concrete support for how the session could work?

options.text: It will be very, very good.
Students could listen to one short song in a supervised room and discuss what they noticed.
options.rationale: Plausible process tied to the session.

options.text: Music is music, and everyone knows music.

supplemental.title: Unity is not word count
supplemental.prompt: Your paragraph has one clear point, a matching reason and example, and no unrelated sentences; it is shorter than a suggested word range.
supplemental.question: Which action is best before adding anything?

options.text: Add an unrelated story until it reaches exactly 100 words.
Re-check the task and decide whether any necessary idea is missing; keep it concise if nothing is missing.
options.rationale: Meaning and coverage are more important than arbitrary length.

options.text: Delete the topic sentence because short paragraphs cannot have one.

aiLens: Review unity and relevance by citing exact saved sentences, not word counts. Ask about off-task content only if it exists. Accept varied order and multifunctional sentences; do not require a separate conclusion.
